speaker: Sean Carroll
title: Sean Carroll: General Relativity, Quantum Mechanics, Black Holes & Aliens (#428)
question: In complexity science, why do simple cellular automata fall short as models of how real-world physical complexity emerges?
guest: Cellular automata come from imagining a very simple configuration, like a set of ones and zeros along a line, and inventing a rule to evolve it in time. Generally, the simplest ones have each block of three ones and zeros deterministically go to either a one or a zero. What was discovered by various people, including Stephen Wolfram, is that some of these cellular automata have the feature that you start from almost nothing, like 000010000, let it rip, and it becomes wildly complex. That is very provocative and interesting. It's also not how physics works at all, because physics conserves information—you can go forward or backwards. These cellular automata do not. They're not reversible in any sense. You've built in an arrow of time: you have a starting point, and then you evolve. What I'm interested in is seeing how in the real world, with the real laws of physics and underlying reversibility, macroscopic irreversibility from entropy and the arrow of time leads to complexity. I think that's an answerable question, and I don't think cellular automata are really helping us in that one.

points.core: Standard cellular automata update rules are irreversible because they destroy prior information.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Simple cellular automata show that complex patterns can arise from simple rules, but they fall short as models of physical emergence because their idealizations strip out most of what drives complexity in nature.

They are closed, deterministic systems running on a fixed lattice with a global clock, synchronous updates and discrete states. Real systems are open and driven far from equilibrium by flows of energy and matter. They are also noisy, continuous and asynchronous, and they obey conservation laws, microscopic reversibility and symmetries that most automata ignore. Much automaton behaviour is fragile: add noise or asynchronous updating and the intricate structures often vanish, whereas natural complexity is robust.

Their rules are also fixed from outside. In nature, structures feed back on the rules themselves, building hierarchies of new levels with new effective laws, and in living systems adaptation and selection keep generating novelty. Automata typically plateau at one level of organization and do not show open-ended evolution.

Finally, interesting behaviour often depends on hand-picked rules and initial conditions, and resemblance of patterns is not explanation: an automaton rarely yields quantitative, testable predictions tied to measurable physical mechanisms.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Simple cellular automata show that intricate patterns and universal computation can arise from minimal local rules, yet they omit the physical mechanisms that actually generate real-world complexity. They rely on a rigid discrete lattice, a global synchronous clock, and fixed, externally imposed rules, whereas real physical and biological systems obey continuous symmetries and conservation laws while exhibiting multiscale feedback, in which emergent macro-structures dynamically constrain lower-level interactions. Moreover, classic cellular automata are closed, deterministic, and brittle: slight thermal noise or asynchronous updating typically destroys their delicate patterns. Natural complexity instead arises in open thermodynamic systems driven far from equilibrium, where energy flows and dissipation actively stabilize robust, hierarchical organization against constant perturbation. Finally, cellular automata often conflate pseudorandomness and computational irreducibility with genuine structural complexity, and because their state spaces and update rules are static, they fail to capture the open-endedness through which real evolving systems continually generate new constraints, interactions, and functional possibilities.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Simple cellular automata like Wolfram's Rule 110 or Conway's Game of Life show that very simple local rules can produce intricate, even computationally universal, behavior. But that only proves complexity is *possible*. It doesn't explain how complexity actually arises in nature.

The main problem is that CAs leave out the physics that drives real self-organization. Their space, time and states are discrete, and every cell updates in lockstep on a fixed grid, so they lack continuous symmetries such as rotation and Lorentz invariance. Most CAs are also irreversible and have no conservation laws, energy, or thermodynamics. Real complex structures, from convection cells to living organisms, form in open systems held far from equilibrium, where energy flows through them and gets dissipated. CAs have nothing like those flows, constraints, or entropy production.

The rules are also chosen by hand rather than derived from physical law, so they predict little and explain little about any specific phenomenon. Finally, CAs mostly produce complex-looking patterns rather than adaptive, functional organization built up in layers. They can't model history, feedback across different scales, or rules that change over time, all of which shape the complexity we see in physics and biology.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Simple cellular automata show that intricate patterns can arise from minimal local rules, yet they miss several mechanisms central to real-world physical complexity. Most notably, they operate on rigid, discrete lattices with synchronous global clocks and fixed, short-range interactions, whereas physical systems evolve asynchronously in continuous space and time with long-range forces and shifting interaction networks. Standard cellular automata also lack fundamental physical constraints such as energy and momentum conservation, thermal noise, and nonequilibrium thermodynamic flows; in nature, self-organization typically depends on open systems dissipating free energy across gradients rather than closed, deterministic rule tables. Furthermore, their microscopic rules and state spaces are permanently fixed, preventing the open-ended emergence of new degrees of freedom, hierarchical organization, and multiscale feedback, where macroscopic structures reshape the boundary conditions and constraints acting on lower-level components. Consequently, while cellular automata are valuable conceptual metaphors for computational irreducibility and pattern formation, they cannot capture how physically grounded, adaptive, and hierarchically organized complexity actually emerges and persists in nature.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Simple cellular automata show how local rules can generate complex patterns. Their limitation is that a complex pattern alone tells us little about which physical mechanisms produced it. In a typical simple automaton, cells occupy a fixed grid, have a few possible states, and update in lockstep. In physical systems, interactions can unfold at different rates and across many scales. The structures that emerge can also change how the system evolves, as when a growing crystal redirects the flow of heat and material around it.

A cellular automaton can model such processes if its rules capture the relevant physics and its predictions agree with observations. The appearance of complexity by itself only establishes that the rules can generate it.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer: Simple cellular automata show that a few local rules can generate intricate patterns. Their limitation is that an intricate pattern alone does not explain the physical process that produced it. A cellular automaton typically starts with a fixed grid, a small set of possible states, and a prescribed update rule. In a real system, energy flows, material properties, and interactions across scales can determine which structures form and whether they persist. For example, a rule might produce stripes that resemble ripples in sand. To explain the ripples, it would also need to capture how wind moves grains and how the growing ridges redirect the wind. The test is whether the model predicts how the ripples change when the wind changes.
